name: Nsenga
confidence_why: Nsenga is tonal by every modern source, but the record's other leg, no word stress, rests on one hedged survey sentence (Kashoki & Mann 1978, generalising over Zambian languages with Cewa as the example) and the silence of a 21-page sketch of one dialect (Simango 2006), while the most detailed Nsenga-specific description in hand, Ranger 1928, states a penultimate-stress system with alternating secondary stress and stress shift off object infixes; that is an old, non-specialist source and it loses, and Miti 2001 is only known second-hand, so this is a clear winner with few sources and a mild disagreement, not a clear consensus.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Nsenga has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so nothing can be contradicted. This work adds only that the prosodic system is treated as tone (Nsenga proper: H/L/F after Miti 2001, secondhand; Kunda: tone limited, predictable, non-contrastive in the author's data) and that it is silent on word stress. Note the variety: the primary description is of Kunda, which Glottolog files as dialect kund1254 under nsen1242 but which the author explicitly treats as an independent language (Guthrie N42) that 'should not be confused to be a dialect of.. Nsenga' (p. 3).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The sketch never mentions word stress, accent or prominence for Kunda or Nsenga (the only occurrence of 'stress' in the whole text, p. 7, is a summary of Horton 1937 on Luvale). Its prosody chapter consists of a tone section saying that Kunda makes 'limited use of tone', that tone 'seems to be predictable', that no lexical or grammatical minimal pairs by tone were found, and that the study therefore sets tone aside (p. 30; restated on p. 31: 'tone could not signal any semantic distinction between words'). For Nsenga proper it reports secondhand, after Miti (2001), a tone language with H, L and surface falling tones used for lexical and grammatical distinctions (p. 9). Vowel length: 'Vowel length in Kunda is distinctive and occurs in at least four vowels /ii, ee, aa, uu/ though not phonemically contrastive' and is 'derived through fusion and coalescence' (p. 24); nothing is said about penultimate lengthening or any positional prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; on tone, the author says tone is limited/predictable in Kunda with no minimal pairs found, whereas Miti (2001) is cited as describing Cinsenga (Nsenga) as using pitch lexically and grammatically
new_statements.identity_note: Zemba (2015) describes Kunda, spoken in Mambwe district, Eastern Province, Zambia (six native-speaker consultants; about 6,760 speakers per the 2010 census). Glottolog lists Kunda as dialect kund1254 of Nsenga nsen1242, which is why the work is filed under this item, but the author states (p. 3) that Kunda is Guthrie N42 and 'an independent language which should not be confused to be a dialect of other similar languages, particularly Nsenga'. Statements about Nsenga proper (Cinsenga of Chipata district) in this work are secondhand summaries of Miti (2001).

readall_conflicts: No source opened states a word-stress rule for Nsenga, so there is no stress conflict. There is a mild tension on tone: Zemba (2015: 30) finds tone in Kunda 'limited', 'predictable' and without minimal pairs, while the same work summarises Miti (2001) as describing Cinsenga (Nsenga proper) as a tone language with H, L and falling tones used lexically and grammatically (p. 9); this is a difference between varieties or analyses, not a statement about stress. Separately, the file already held by the project from the earlier reading (Appendix 1, PDF page 21) lists 'N41 Nsenga Zambia' among 'Languages with PL [penultimate lengthening] that have lost the PB *V/VV contrast', which is compatible with Zemba's report that Kunda vowel length is not phonemically contrastive and arises from fusion/coalescence (p. 24), but Zemba says nothing about penultimate lengthening.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: both Kashoki & Mann 1978 passages (pp. 63-64 penult lengthening in all Eastern Province languages; p. 70 syllables evenly stressed, penult force = lengthening, stress non-distinctive, every syllable carries tone) and the Ranger 1928 p. vii/fn. 5 passages are verbatim at the stated locators in the text files we hold, and Simango 2006 (held PDF) independently states for Nsenga itself that penult lengthening is non-phonemic and that H/L/Falling tone is lexical and grammatical, with no stress or accent anywhere in the sketch. Hyman 2013 (downloaded now, open) lists N41 Nsenga among penultimate-lengthening languages, consistent.
